title: Stack vs heap
description: Understand how the stack and heap work, and when each is used for memory allocation.

data.text: Every running program needs memory. Your computer organizes that memory into two main regions: the stack and the heap. Each has different rules, speed, and lifetime behavior. Understanding when and why each is used is fundamental to writing efficient programs.

The stack is a region of memory that stores local variables and function call information. It is called a stack because it works exactly like a stack of plates: you can only add or remove from the top. When a function is called, its variables are pushed onto the stack. When the function returns, those variables are automatically removed.

data.title: Stack characteristics
items: Grows and shrinks automatically with function calls
Fixed maximum size (usually a few megabytes)
Stores local variables, parameters, and return addresses

data.title: Stack allocation in C
data.content: Local variables are placed on the stack and disappear when the function exits.

data.text: The heap is a much larger pool of memory used for data that must outlive a single function call. Unlike the stack, heap memory does not get cleaned up automatically. You must explicitly request it (allocation) and later release it (deallocation). If you forget to release memory, it leaks — the program keeps it forever even though it is no longer needed.

data.title: Memory leaks
data.text: In languages like C and C++, forgetting to free heap memory causes leaks. In C# and Java, garbage collection automatically reclaims heap objects that are no longer reachable, but leaks can still occur if references are held unnecessarily.

data.title: Heap allocation in C
data.content: malloc requests memory from the heap, and free releases it back.

data.title: Memory management by language
items: C and C++ — manual stack and heap management with malloc/free or new/delete
C# — stack for local value types and references; heap for reference types; garbage collected
Java — stack for primitives and references; heap for objects; garbage collected
Python — stack for references; heap for objects; reference counted with cyclic GC

items.question: Can the stack run out of space?
items.answer: Yes. Deep recursion can overflow the stack because each recursive call adds a new frame. This is called a stack overflow.

items.question: Is heap allocation always slower?
items.answer: Usually yes, because finding a free block and managing fragmentation takes more work. Some allocators are very fast, but the stack is almost always faster.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: The stack is fast, automatic, and limited in size
The heap is large, flexible, and requires explicit management or garbage collection
Value types and local variables typically use the stack
Objects and dynamically sized data typically use the heap
data.takeaway: Knowing how memory is organized helps you avoid stack overflows, reduce heap allocations, and write more efficient code.
